paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the stratigraphy of Uan Afuda, the Epipalaeolithic level is characterised by a predominance of mouflon in the faunal remains but it is only in the successive Mesolithic layer that the use of the cave becomes more intensive (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1998). This phase differs from the previous one revealing evidence for a broad spectrum of resources including large and small mammals. Apart from mouflon, several wild species were hunted such as golden jackal, hartebeest, hedgehog, porcupine and others (Corridi 1998). As the archaeological remains seem to suggest, in the Mesolithic phase Uan Afuda was inhabited for long periods during the year. The most striking characteristic of this stratigraphic unit is the massive accumulation of animal dung and undecomposed plants alternating with ashes, charcoal and faunal remains.

paragraphs.source_en: Whereas wild animals could have flocked together in the cave, they could not have introduced the fodder. The presence of plant remains and charcoal as well as the occurrence of archaeological material emphasises the contemporaneous presence of wild animals and humans in the 9th millennium BP (Di Lernia 1999). The micromorphological analysis of the sediments in the atrial deposit and in the inner part of the cave revealed the presence of spherulites and coprolites, formations indicating ovicaprids, which was interpreted as the management of mouflon (Di Lernia 1999).

paragraphs.source_en: Why did these hunter-gatherers keep mouflon in the area they inhabited? The considerable quantity of the dung suggests that the presence of mouflon in the cave was rather long. Can we suggest a predomestication nearly 1,000 years before the attested pastoral occupation in the Acacus? Most scholars agree that domestication of Ammotragus lervia did not occur in such an early period (Hachid 1998; Di Lernia 1999; Aumassip 2004). They rather suggest a management and taming of mouflon as part of a gradual process leading towards food-production in the Pastoral period.
